summary:
Same-sex conduct is not a criminal offence in Guinea-Bissau. The penal code introduced by Decree 4/93 in 1993 omits same-sex offences, and the U.S. Department of State's 2011 and 2012 human rights reports both record that consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised.

There is no transgender legal framework of any kind. No legal gender recognition procedure exists, so a visitor's identity documents carry the sex marker assigned at birth, with no domestic route to alter it before or during travel, and no statute addresses gender marker change at all.

The state recognises no partnership or marriage for couples read as same-sex under local law. No statute provides for such recognition, and official practice on family-size government housing treats those couples as single-person households rather than as couples.

No anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation or gender identity. The U.S. Department of State's 2012 report states plainly that the country's anti-discrimination laws do not apply to LGBT individuals, while recording no official discrimination against them in access to health care, employment or education, and no reported violent incidents or human-rights abuses targeting people on that basis in the reporting period covered by that report.

Sexual orientation and gender identity do appear in one piece of protective legislation. Article 5 of the Law against Domestic Violence (Law No. 6/2014) provides that all victims, regardless of sexual orientation, enjoy the fundamental rights inherent to human dignity and are guaranteed equal opportunities to a life free from violence as well as physical and mental health.

The reported picture of societal treatment is contested and dated. The U.S. Department of State's 2011 report documents societal stigma against LGBT people, and its 2012 report notes that social taboos against homosexuality sometimes restrict freedom to express sexual orientation while finding society relatively tolerant of consensual same-sex conduct. In 2018 a local NGO director stated that there had been some cases of violence targeting people based on sexual orientation or gender identity and that legal protections for LGBTI people are absent.
tangentialFactors:
A 2010 Pew Research Center survey of 19 African countries placed Guinea-Bissau among the more tolerant cases: nine percent of respondents said homosexual behaviour was morally acceptable and fifteen percent said it was not an issue. These are historical figures from a survey that closed in 2010 and measure attitudes to homosexuality generally, not treatment of trans people, and no comparable current survey appears in the sources.

Guinea-Bissau signed the 2008 UN statement on sexual orientation and gender identity, a diplomatic position that carries no domestic legal force.

An overview of the country's LGBT situation describes no visible LGBT social scene, so a visitor should not expect venues or organised community gathering points. One country guide assigns a travel-safety score of 34 out of 100, which is that publication's own rating rather than a documented finding.

The sources record no youth-specific or minor-specific findings on health access, schooling or travel, and nothing specific to trans or LGBTQ minors.
localsOnly:
Government housing allowances are restricted to heterosexual married couples, who alone qualify for family-size government housing; same-sex couples receive the single-person allotment. The U.S. Department of State recorded this rule in both its 2011 and its 2012 reports, and it is applied through civil-service guidelines rather than through a published statute.

Adoption law does not address the position of LGBTQ applicants. A French government guidance page states that single and married people are eligible to adopt without saying whether LGBTQ people are disqualified, so the status of placements involving them is unresolved in the sources.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable to residents as well as visitors: there is no procedure, no statute and no administrative route by which a person born in Guinea-Bissau can change the sex marker on domestic documents.

The absence of any anti-discrimination provision covering sexual orientation or gender identity means residents who face refusal of service, employment or health care on those grounds have no statutory claim to bring, notwithstanding the equality language of Article 5 of Law No. 6/2014 in the specific context of domestic violence.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether LGBT people face greater violence than the general population is unresolved. The sources offer only two dated and conflicting observations: a 2012 government report finding no reported violent incidents on that basis, and a 2018 statement from a local NGO director reporting some such cases. No figures, rates or denominators accompany either, and no trans-specific violence data of any kind appears in the inventory.

Whether LGBTQ applicants are barred from adoption is not sourced; the available guidance is silent rather than permissive or prohibitive.

The most recent human-rights reporting in the inventory is from 2012, with the NGO statement from 2018. Current enforcement practice, any legislative drafting after those dates, and present-day police treatment of gender-nonconforming visitors are not sourced here.

No entry, visa or border-screening rules specific to trans travellers, and no documented instances of document-marker flagging or secondary screening on the basis of gender presentation, appear in the sources.
